of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) can be explained by changes in the central source's luminosity.  However, the remarkable, large-scale jet variability observed in some radio-active galactic nuclei, such as BL Lac objects, is thought to result from the interaction between relativistic jets and local density fluctuations within the host galaxy's intracluster medium.  We present a novel, semi-analytical model that simulates these density fluctuations, focusing on the important role that both the amplitude and scale of these fluctuations play in determining the pattern of jet variability.  By applying this model to a sample of FLRQs and BL Lac objects, we found that the observed variability characteristics are consistent with the Airere-Ripere-Bondi (BZB) jet model and support the idea that these sources are locally accelerating jets.  Additionally, we discovered that the total energy carried by relativistic jets accounts for approximately 0.1% of a radio-active galactic nucleus's rest mass energy, which is in line with existing observations.  This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the optical to radio variability behavior of active galactic nuclei, offering a practical tool for predicting the variability patterns of radio-active galactic nuclei based on their optical and UV characteristics.  We make our model publicly available on the web to facilitate its use by the scientific community.  Furthermore, we propose the implementation of a dedicated variability monitoring program for radio-active galactic nuclei to aid in the discovery of distant radio-active galactic nuclei and the study of extreme radio-active galactic nuclei.  Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this study in a variety of fields, including a proposed mission concept for a wide-field, high-time-resolution radio telescope capable of detecting radio-active galactic nuclei at a z of 10. Unlike typical Gaussian process methods, which require smoothness assumptions, our model called the Local Gaussian Process (LGProcess) focuses on local properties.  This is because within state space regions with similar characteristics, it acts similarly to a Gaussian process, yet diverges in areas with notable changes.  These unique properties make the LGProcess suitable for use in recursive estimation algorithms, allowing it to be applied in scenarios with limited information, and enabling the estimation of both the state and the model's uncertainty.  By incorporating this model into a recursive filter, we can efficiently manage partially known linear dynamic systems.  An important aspect of this model is that it provides a posterior variance that represents the uncertainty within the estimates, enabling the implementation of consensus algorithms based on the most confident estimates.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of the LGProcess through a simulation involving a group of partially informed agents attempting to reconstruct a signal, and a theoretical advantage proof showing that the LGProcess is at least as accurate as other models in a key performance metric.  This research has practical applications in the control and management of distributed dynamic systems, and can be applied in a variety of scenarios including sensor networks, robotic formations, and data collection platforms.  One potential area of interest involves the optimization of payoff functions within dynamic games, as the LGProcess can be utilized to tackle the challenges associated with the information asymmetry.  Additionally, the research contributes to the development of the Gaussian Processes framework by introducing a novel, locally consistent variation that can be used in the creation of more complex, composite models.  These findings have implications for the use of Gaussian Process models in the regulation and control of dynamic systems with partially known dynamics. This research aims to address this challenge by exploring the tidal dissipation mechanism, which is responsible for the characteristic signal feature in binary neutron star mergers.  characterized by inflammatory lesions, axonal damage, and progressive cognitive
 impairments.  The etiology of MS is multifactorial, involving environmental and
 genetic risk factors.  One of the most significant environmental risk factors is
 vitamin D deficiency, which has been linked to an increased risk of developing MS
 and the progression of the disease.  The exact mechanism by which vitamin D
 influences MS remains unclear; however, research suggests that it affects immune
 regulation and inflammation within the CNS.  Vitamin D receptors are present in
 oligodendrocytes, which are responsible for myelination, indicating a direct role
 in myelin formation and repair.  Animal models have shown that vitamin D supplementation
 can reduce inflammation and promote remyelination, providing a potential
 therapeutic approach for treating MS.  Furthermore, studies have demonstrated a
 positive correlation between vitamin D levels and cognitive function in MS patients,
 suggesting a possible vitamin D-based treatment for improving cognitive impairments.  
  In this review, we examine the current evidence regarding the relationship between
 vitamin D and MS, focusing on the molecular mechanisms involved, the effects of
 vitamin D on myelination, and its potential as a therapeutic option for treating
 MS and associated cognitive impairments.  We also discuss the limitations of
 existing research and propose future directions for investigating this topic.  
  The research highlights the critical role of vitamin D in myelination and its
 implications for treating MS and cognitive impairments.  It is essential to conduct
 further in vitro and in vivo studies to fully understand the mechanisms by which
 vitamin D affects myelination and to explore its therapeutic potential for MS.  
  The findings of this review advocate for incorporating vitamin D into the current
 treatment plans for MS patients and for conducting large-scale epidemiological
 studies to establish a clear link between vitamin D deficiency and MS.  It is also
 crucial to develop more accurate methods for measuring vitamin D levels and to
 investigate the effects of vitamin D on myelination in humans.  Overall, the research
 suggests that vitamin D has a significant influence on myelination and could be a
 promising treatment option for treating MS and associated cognitive impairments.  
  The review contributes to the current understanding of the relationship between
 vitamin D and MS, providing a foundation for the development of vitamin D-based
 treatments and the implementation of preventive measures against vitamin D
 deficiency.  It is essential to conduct further research on the topic

At low transverse momenta, the source is elliptical, aligning with the reaction plane, whereas, at higher transential momenta, it becomes more circular. To better understand these unusual IMFs, we performed a theoretical examination of the relationship between the stellar initial mass function (IMF) and the molecular cloud properties.  Using high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations of molecular cloud evolution, we found that the IMF is directly correlated with both the local gas density and the cloud's total mass.  A power-law relationship is observed between the IMF slope and the average cloud density, with a beta-value of -1.35 for low densities and 2.35 for high densities.  Additionally, we discovered a linear relationship between the characteristic mass and the cloud's average density, with a proportionality constant of 0.64.  These findings are in agreement with existing theoretical models and provide a fundamental understanding of the IMF's variation within different molecular cloud environments.  Our research suggests that the stellar IMF is an intrinsic property of molecular cloud evolution, influenced by local physical conditions and cloud morphology, and is not determined by birthplace environment or the presence of massive stars.  By establishing a theoretical framework for the IMF's shape, we aim to integrate this knowledge into chemical and radiative transfer models of galaxy evolution, with the goal of accurately predicting optical and near-infrared spectra of local and distant galaxies.  This research contributes to our overall effort to mature the "physical IMF" approach and explore its applications in understanding the evolution of galaxies. (Very Long Baseline Interferometry) system located in the Orion Nebula, which we have dubbed "ONRAGE."  This system aims to form high-resolution images of the region by observing methanol masers and studying the physics of molecular collapse and star formation.  We have carried out the necessary source stability measurements using existing VLBI networks and have developed a data reduction protocol.  Based on our calculations, we anticipate that the ONRAGE system will achieve a sensitivity of 10 microJy within a 5.5km/s bandwidth and an integration time of 8 hours.  This sensitivity will enable the detection of methanol masers with densities of ~10^9 cm^-3 and temperatures of ~10K.  We believe that the ONRAGE system will contribute significantly to our understanding of how stars form, particularly in the context of the Orion Nebula's unique conditions.  Additionally, we discuss the possibility of using this system to search for 6.7GHz methanol masers as signs of forming brown dwarfs.  We have also calculated the stability requirements for phase reference vessels in VLBI observations and propose the construction of a second VLBI system in the 6.7GHz band to observe 6.4 to 6.9GHz transitory masers associated with massive star formation.  We conclude that the most feasible option is to observe these transitory masers using existing VLBI networks and suggest the use of wide-field radio telescopes to observe the accompanying optical and near-infrared emission.  Finally, we discuss the possibility of using the ATOMI project's wide-field radio telescope to observe these transitory masers and the accompanying optical and near-infrared emission.  We propose the development of a wide-field radio telescope with a field of view of at least 10x10 arcminutes and an sensitivity of 10^-7 Jy/Hz for observations of 6.7GHz methanol masers and 10^-8 Jy/Hz for observations of 6.4 to 6.9GHz transitory masers. to investigate dynamic non-local relativistic quantum fluctuations and their impact on cosmological scalar field fluctuations during an early epoch when the universe was still evolving. As the fluctuations evolved, some became classical fields, ultimately giving rise to structure in the universe through gravitational effects and the formation of particles.  Methods. We utilize a quantum non-local relativistic field framework to analyze fluctuations in a simple scalar field model, focusing on a simplified cosmological setting.  Results. Building on the previous paper, we examine the evolution of fluctuations in a simple scalar field model, with a focus on non-local effects and their impact on the curve of quantum fluctuations in phase-space.  Conclusion. Non-local effects on fluctuations are found to be insignificant in quantum fluctuations, but are crucial in converting quantum fluctuations into classical fields.  Remarks. Future papers in this series will explore the evolution of fluctuations in a full non-linear representation and the transformation of quantum fluctuations into classical fields.  Context. This research is part of a larger project that aims to provide a microscopic understanding of cosmological structure formation through the formation of particles and the growth of gravitational effects on classical fields.  Subject. This research contributes to our understanding of the initial stages of structure formation in the universe.  Keywords. This research involves the study of dynamic non-local relativistic quantum fluctuations in cosmological scalar field models, the evolution of fluctuations, the formation of classical fields, and the development of gravitational effects on classical fields. Unlike the classical KdV equation, this variant includes a term that represents an external force acting on the line.  The goal of this research was to investigate the existence of global solutions, with the added constraint that the initial condition is extremely small.  To resolve this issue, we employ the method of constructive proof, specifically the perturbation technique of Birkhoff-Moura.  Additionally, we utilize the conservation laws of the equation, specifically the conservation law for the energy and the conservation law for the momentum.  With these tools in hand, we demonstrate that extremely small initial conditions result in global solutions that decay over time.  Furthermore, we show that these solutions are infinitely differentiable and that they converge to a specific constant value as time progresses.  To conclude, we provide a straightforward method for calculating this constant value.  This research contributes to the ongoing effort to study the KdV equation equipped with an external force and an initial condition.  It also extends previous research on the classical KdV equation, which typically involves initial conditions that are smooth but not necessarily extremely small.  This study is relevant to various physical phenomena, including ocean wave dynamics, sound wave propagation, and shallow water wave motion.  It is also pertinent to mathematical research on the KdV equation, which serves as a fundamental model for studying solitonic behavior in nonlinear wave equations. Using SPIRE/PACS observations from the Herschel space observatory, we found that the dust disk radius in these galaxies is significantly enhanced in regions closest to the central engines, and that a possible connection exists between this enhancement and the formation of young stars.  A possible explanation for this phenomenon is the influence of starburst-driven outflows on dust disk morphology, which can heat dust in outer regions, making it less visible to observations.  Another possibility is that outflows compress and shape dust disks in a way that makes them more prone to cooling and density increases in inner regions.  Both processes might contribute to the observed dust disk features by creating conditions favorable for star formation.  This research is the first to provide detailed observations of dust disk inflation in distant starbursting galaxies, and its findings are consistent with current theoretical models of galaxy evolution, which suggest that outflows play a crucial role in shaping dust disks and facilitating star formation.  This study also contributes to our understanding of how dust disks evolve in response to starburst activity, and how this evolution impacts the formation of stars and heavy elements in the universe.  Furthermore, the research offers observational evidence in support of the idea that outflows are a key factor in shaping dust disks, and can be used to test and develop theoretical models of galaxy evolution.  This research is relevant to various fields of astrophysics, including galaxy evolution, star formation, and the creation of heavy elements. This proposed XANs method aims to offer transparent and reliable guidance on the most appropriate treatments and actions in high-stakes situations.  To evaluate the proposed XANs approach, a pilot study was conducted involving five real-world clinical decision-making scenarios. One scenario involved a patient with sepsis, where the network acknowledged the importance of blood pressure but discounted its weight compared to other vital signs when making decisions.  Another scenario involved a patient with acute kidney injury, where the network recognized the significance of electrolyte levels in determining the best course of action.  The proposed XANs method has the potential to revolutionize the way healthcare professionals utilize AI in critical care by providing a clear understanding of the underlying reasoning behind treatment suggestions.  Healthcare providers can utilize the proposed XANs approach to create their own, dataset-independent, decision-support systems for various clinical conditions and scenarios.   A key challenge in managing a product flow network is determining the shortest path between products, as it's essential for reducing waste, promoting recycling, and facilitating the reuse of products.
  Although the shortest path problem is a well-studied issue in graph theory, its solution can vary depending on the algorithm used and the data structure employed.

To further assess the quality of the proposed system, we conducted an online survey involving 200 participants from diverse cultural backgrounds. The outcomes align with the proposed classification, suggesting that it effectively mirrors human perception of emoji semantics. Given the small transverse sizes of jets, we utilize a 3+1D ideal gluon hydrodynamics model, evolving the junctions of gluing collapsed initial conditions over proper time, and solving for gluon jet distributions.  We compare and contrast our results with existing data from both 200 GeV and 13 TeV heavy-ion collisions, finding overall agreement on jet shape modifications and agreeing with experimental findings on pion multiplicity distributions.  Notably, we observe slight discrepancies in jet shape modifications for 200 GeV and 13 TeV heavy-ion collisions, attributing these differences to varying heavy ion densities and initial condition transverse profiles. Finally, we propose a simple phenomenological model to estimate gluon jet collisionality, offering a possible approach for incorporating jet hydrodynamics into event generators. However, with unbalanced data, the majority class's influence can be detrimental, and the minority class's importance may be undervalued.  To address this, unweighted methods like Majority Reducts and Formal Concept Analysis have been proposed; they prioritize the minority class but overlook the majority class's information.  In contrast, a new approach called Bi-Class Reducts extends the concept of descriptive learning to weigh the importance of classes.  This approach is more versatile, as it preserves key properties like minimality and generality, and can incorporate various measure options like information gain and absolute precision. Theoretical analyses demonstrate the optimal Bi-Class Reduct's existence, its uniqueness in certain conditions, and its accuracy and generality bounds.  Additionally, an empirical study on real-world datasets shows the superiority of Bi-Class Reducts over unweighted methods.  This research provides a foundation for using Bi-Class Reducts in descriptive learning, especially in tasks like classification rule creation and feature selection. In such networks, information diffusion occurs when nodes that have already learned certain information share it with neighboring nodes that are still unaware of it.  Over time, this process spreads knowledge across the network, and a way to measure the effectiveness of this process is by calculating the largest amount of information that can be transmitted within a given time frame.  This problem is equivalent to determining the largest number of discrete colors that can be spread throughout the network after a specified number of coloring attempts.  This specific problem is known as the "missing color problem," and it can be formulated as follows: Given an integer k and a graph G, find the largest number of colors that can be applied to the vertices of G such that no vertex with color c has a neighbor with the same color c.  This problem is proven to be NP-hard even for restricted cases of specific network shapes.  However, for a particular variant where nodes are arranged in a one-dimensional line and there's no more than one color missing between adjacent nodes, an efficient algorithm has been established to solve it.  Building upon this information, an algorithm can be created to calculate the largest number of discrete colors transmitted within a given time frame in a ring-shaped network where nodes are initially uninfected and information is transmitted between adjacent nodes.  This specific scenario can also be framed as the "contact tracing problem," and it can be solved in less than one second for instances of 10^5 nodes.  In a network of 10^5 nodes where information is transmitted between adjacent nodes and there's no more than one color missing between adjacent nodes, the largest number of discrete colors transmitted within a given time frame can be calculated in less than 2.5 seconds and the largest number of infected nodes within a given time frame for the largest number of discrete colors can be calculated in less than 5 seconds.  This data can be displayed on a computer in less than 10 seconds.  This solution can be applied to a computer within a few tens of milliseconds to a network of 10^6 nodes. Despite its widespread adoption, research on WiFi fingerprinting has started to wane, with many recent conferences featuring significantly reduced publication numbers.  To better understand the decline of research interest in this area, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the literature on WiFi fingerprinting, exploring its foundations, current limitations, and the reasons behind the decreasing publication numbers. Our research suggests that the RNN-IFM technique has real-world applicability potential, with possible use cases including large-scale outdoor events, crowded urban areas, and emergency response situations. As the star is drawn towards the black hole, it experiences significant tidal forces, causing it to spin and orbit in a way that is highly unstable.  In this research, we examine the initial instability that arises when the star's spin and orbital angular momentum are misaligned. Furthermore, we observe that the instability is not uniformly distributed across the star, instead manifesting more significantly towards the side facing the black hole.  To better understand this phenomenon, we compare the growth rate of the instability by varying the star's composition and size.  Surprisingly, we find that the instability's growth rate is unaffected by changes in the star's composition but is highly sensitive to changes in size.  To further analyze the instability, we evaluate the growth rate's curvature at the star's surface.  Notably, we discover that the curvature's sign is positive towards the side facing the black hole, indicating that the instability is driven by non-axisymmetric modes that are baroclinic. As this method involves using measured flow data to close Navier-Stokes equations, its accuracy relies on the quality of the input data.  Given the complex nature of turbulence, even small errors in data generation phase can have considerable effects on closure results, making precise measurement crucial.  In an effort to evaluate the stability of data-driven modeling, researchers have examined the initial data's variability by performing small amendments to the input conditions and analyzing how closure solutions respond.  However, a comprehensive assessment of the model's stability entails evaluating the outcome's sensitivity to changes in both initial conditions and the problem's evolution, which is not currently possible with direct numerical simulations of turbulence.  To address this gap, we propose using a linear stability analysis to assess the stability of closure equations, which provides a precise measure of stability in relation to both initial conditions and the flow's evolution.  We demonstrate that data-driven modeling is inherently unstable when using LES or DNS resolutions and propose several possible causes, including the cancellation of eddy viscosity terms and the absence of slow velocity scale evolution.  Furthermore, we observe that the analysis can identify physically irrelevant solutions that direct numerical simulations may yield, illustrating the theory's practical applicability.  To further explore the stability of closure equations, we utilize the linear stability framework in a periodic box simulation of isotropic turbulence, which shows that the model's instability is linked to the presence of shear and/or rotation.  We conclude that data-driven turbulence modeling is inherently unstable, which has implications for its implementation and the development of alternative closure models.  Additionally, we recognize that a linear stability analysis can help refine the models by eliminating unstable solutions, which may also contribute to the development of more stable models.  To facilitate this, we provide an open-source code implementation of the linear stability analysis on GitHub.  Finally, we propose several possible avenues for future research, including the investigation of the linear stability conditions for different turbulence scenarios and the exploration of more sophisticated stability assessment methods.  To facilitate this, we have contributed several turbulence simulation datasets to the Turbulence Database Project.  We believe that a thorough examination of the stability of turbulence models is essential for the advancement of data-driven turbulence research and the development of more effective models in the future.  To achieve this, we suggest a unified framework for evaluating the stability of turbulence models, which involves assessing the growth rate of perturbations in relation to both initial conditions and the flow's evolution, and propose several possible assessment methods.

  Although remote sensing technology offers various advantages in disaster information acquisition, its effectiveness is hampered
  by cloud cover, which is a significant constraint in areas with high rainfall and frequent fog.

  and significantly improve the accuracy of disaster information acquisition compared to traditional methods.

  remote sensing images, leading to a 23.9% increase in the total number of effective images and a 90.5% reduction in the
  cost of image acquisition.

We explore the concept of $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry in relation to a specific model consisting of two coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equations. Contrary to the single nonlinear Schrödinger equation, we find that the presence of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric complex potentials does not guarantee a stable spectrum for the combined system. To analyze the system's stability, we compute the eigenvalues at the point of $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry breaking. In the special case of a Gaussian potential, we derive a precise condition for determining the stability based on the system parameters. What's more, we obtain a simplified criterion that can be applied to approximate the real part of the complex eigenvalue through a numerical iteration process. By applying this process initially with a sinusoidal potential, we obtain a refined boundary for estimating the eigenvalue. To further examine the stability, we compare the computed eigenvalue boundary with another proposed boundary (the phase decay time product) in a realistic optical harmonic generation scenario. Ultimately, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the refined boundary in the scenario of optical harmonic generation in a gas, outperforming the phase decay time product significantly. The computed eigenvalue boundary also correlates with the phase decay time product's decrease in both a single nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the two-coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equation model. Furthermore, we observe that the phase decay time product's decrease is squared in the case of the optical harmonic signal versus the phase decay time product's linear decrease in the pump signal's decay time in the scenario of optical harmonic generation in a gas. A supervised machine learning model was used to examine the emotional tone behind statements made by Iranian and American officials in this specific incident, and similar models have been shown to be effective in determining negative or positive feelings in text based on large datasets.  However, due to the scarcity of existing data on this subject, one dataset from each category was used, and additional data from general political articles was included to help train the models.  The results show that there is a significant difference in how Iranians and Americans feel about each other's blame-worthiness, with most Iranian accusations aimed at the United States and Canada, and vice versa with most American allegations focused on Iran.  Additionally, there is a notable lack of blame directed towards Russia in the news articles, despite existing evidence of Russian involvement in the incident.  This research demonstrates the effectiveness of sentiment analysis in understanding the dynamics of international conflicts and offers several recommendations for using this technique in similar situations.  It also highlights the potential drawbacks of relying on algorithm-driven results and the importance of manually examining the data and models used.  As the amount of globally available information continues to grow, this type of research can help contextually make sense of it, and it is particularly valuable in situations where multiple parties have competing claims and perspectives.  This research is an example of how sentiment analysis can be used to study international conflicts and is available to the public, along with the code and data used, to facilitate this purpose.  It is also available to the academic community to aid in evaluating the effectiveness of this technique in similar situations. This research explores the possibility of differentiating between similar tissue types based on their ultrasonic scattering properties, with a focus on adipose and subcutaneous fat tissues.  In vitro ultrasonic scattering measurements were conducted on both subcutaneous and adipose fat tissues, collected from eight subjects.  The data consists of frequency-based backscattering coefficients (β*), ultrasonic attenuation coefficients (α), and ultrasonic speed values (c).  A statistical analysis was performed to evaluate the differences between the two tissue types, with results indicating that subcutaneous and adipose fat tissues exhibit noticeable differences in ultrasonic scattering properties.  The results also demonstrate that ultrasonic imaging systems primarily detect backscattered signals rather than directly measuring ultrasonic scattering levels.  As a result, the development of imaging processing algorithms is necessary to effectively differentiate between similar tissue types based on ultrasonic scattering properties.  A possible approach involves creating a reference database of ultrasonic scattering property values for various tissue types to facilitate the development of such algorithms.  In the case of distinguishing between subcutaneous and adipose fat tissues, a combination of β*, α, and c values demonstrates the highest differentiation accuracy (R-squared > 0.95) when using a simple linear model.  The research concludes that ultrasonic scattering properties hold promise in differentiating between similar tissue types, with the potential to enhance ultrasonic imaging techniques and enable the development of new applications.  Furthermore, the research suggests that ultrasonic scattering property values can serve as a viable alternative to other techniques for assessing fat tissue characteristics, with implications for various fields including biomedical research, medical imaging, and health condition monitoring. Despite the inherent difficulties, we aim to assess the predictability of local temperature fluctuations in this study, focusing on specific events that can evolve over various timescales. Leveraging a novel approach that evaluates the initial conditions' impact on the outcome of weather patterns, we evaluate the stability of local temperature fluctuations. Our results indicate that fluctuations lasting more than two weeks are generally unstable, whereas shorter-lived fluctuations exhibit varying levels of predictability based on their initial strength and the underlying atmospheric conditions. Notably, we find that the most extreme fluctuations are often the least predictable, suggesting that factors contributing to exceptional heatwaves might be difficult to forecast accurately. By analyzing the relationship between instability and fluctuation timescales, we observe a linear correlation that can be explained by the exponential growth of disturbances in unstable situations. Furthermore, we note that the timescale of fluctuations is directly proportional to the growth rate of disturbances, consistent with the theory of linear instability. Finally, we propose a simple model that approximates the predictability of temperature fluctuations based on the stability of underlying weather patterns, providing a possible framework for improving short-term forecasting outcomes. Despite its importance, determining the electroweak mixing angle is challenging, especially in its low-energy manifestation. To better understand the underlying physics, especially in processes involving quarks, it is crucial to accurately know this parameter. In the standard model and its minimal extension, we determine the average weak charge of up and down quarks to be approximately $0.23 \pm 0.01$. Our objective is to determine the number of reagent and product trajectories within a specific area, without computing every possible initial condition. This problem is equivalent to counting the number of isolated periodic orbits on the Poincaré section of the system's phase space for a particular energy level. Our approach involves using a mapping called the Poincaré-Andreotti operator, which we then employ to count the number of isolated periodic orbits within a given area. This operator returns a value representing the number of isolated periodic orbits on the Poincaré section that contribute to trajectories falling within the specified area. We also explore various characteristics of the Poincaré-Andreotti operator, including its image, domain, and key topological features. Furthermore, we compare the Poincaré-Andreotti operator with another important mapping called the Poincaré-Birkhoff operator, highlighting their differences and similarities. We demonstrate that the Poincaré-Andreotti operator can be applied to a more extensive range of areas than the Poincaré-Birkhoff operator, and we provide a theoretical analysis of how both operators relate to the number of isolated periodic orbits on the Poincaré section. Our research contributes to our understanding of global bifurcations of periodic orbits in Hamiltonian systems and has implications for various fields, including molecular dynamics, celestial mechanics, and nearly integrable Hamiltonian systems. This study investigates the property of between-point sets known as between-point separability, which is essentially identical to the property of separability in metric spaces but has distinct characteristics due to the more general definition of between points.  In between-point spaces, between-point separability can be compared to a related property called density, which is a fundamental characteristic in metric spaces but lacks a direct equivalent in between-point spaces.  This research expands on previous studies by introducing the concept of between-point separability and exploring its relationship with density, demonstrating that in between-point spaces, between-point separability is equivalent to the local density of between-point sets at every point.  Additionally, both properties are found to be topological, and in between-point metric spaces, between-point separability is equivalent to the full coverage of between-point sets that are dense in the space.  This study contributes to the theoretical foundation of between-point spaces by providing a precise characterization of between-point separability, which is anticipated to provide utility in future research.  This research is part of a larger project aimed at developing a theory of between-point sets, which has implications for various areas of mathematics including general topology, geometric measure theory, and the study of specific functions such as harmonic and Newtonian functions. Contrary to the classical gravitational-wave background, this stochastic signal is highly anisotropic, as evidenced by the observed anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background. These discoveries imply that the initial conditions of our universe, influencing both structure formation and gravitational-wave anisotropies, are intricately connected and potentially interrelated.    This research contributes to a comprehensive understanding of the early universe's physical properties, offering a novel perspective on the first phases of cosmic evolution and the formation of large-scale structure. (LISA) is scheduled to observe gravitational waves within the millhertz to kilohertz frequency range. As a result of the vibration of LISA's spacecraft, laser interferometer data is subject to noise that resembles an $f^{-4}$ power spectral density within the detector's lowest frequencies. This noisy behavior is thought to impact the telescope's ability to detect certain types of gravitational wave sources, potentially affecting the statistical analysis of discoveries and the telescope's overall effectiveness. To better understand the influence of LISA's motion on gravitational wave detections, we have performed a local noise simulation, incorporating the actual vibration data from two LISA-like spacecraft. By doing so, we have developed an optimized parameter estimation technique that accounts for the noisy signal phase modulation. Furthermore, we have tested the technique on the merger of two intermediate mass black hole binaries, each with a different mass ratio, and evaluated the effects of the LISA motion on the accuracy of parameter estimates in such events. The results indicate that, in the presence of LISA local noise, the signal amplitude might be affected more significantly than the signal phase. Additionally, we found that the LISA Orphan Search experiment could potentially discover sources with initial black hole masses as small as $10^{-2}M_{\sun}$, and that the statistical analysis of discoveries could be impacted by the noisy signal phase modulation. Finally, we have submitted a proposal to the LISA integration and testing phase to implement a feature that can mitigate the noisy behavior within the detector's lowest frequencies. heavy quark pairs is a key process in heavy ion collisions, and it significantly impacts the behavior of quarks and gluons in these events. While non-relativistic potential models are effective for light quarks, they are insufficient for heavy quarks due to the large energy scales involved. Furthermore, the extension of these models to include the formation of heavy quark pairs is non-trivial. 

  In this work, we present a new approach that seamlessly integrates non-relativistic potential models with the Multiple Scale Approach (MSA), allowing for the spontaneous formation of heavy quark pairs within the quark gluon plasma. The MSA provides a theoretical framework for eliminating the tiny heavy quark mass in intermediate steps, enabling the calculation of the heavy quark pair formation probability and the diffusion coefficient for heavy quarks in a gluon gas. Additionally, we derive closed-form expressions for the diffusion coefficient through momentum relaxation time and the Fock-Vocke procedure, and demonstrate the consistency with existing results. 

  Our results indicate that the heavy quark pair formation probability is of order $(\mu/s)$ for heavy quarks with $\mu$ being the quark mass and $s$ being the energy scale. Moreover, we observe that the diffusion coefficient through momentum relaxation time is consistent with the Fock-Vocke procedure for heavy quarks with masses around $10^{-3}$ GeV. Finally, we provide publicly available numerical code for reproducing the output of the MSA, allowing for the straightforward calculation of the heavy quark pair formation probability and the diffusion coefficient in a gluon gas through a given process, and demonstrate its utility by deriving the diffusion coefficient through momentum relaxation time for heavy quarks in a gluon gas at a temperature of 1 GeV and a energy density of 10 GeV/fm$^3$. Since objects in real-life scenarios often appear in dynamic environments, extending this research to include moving objects is crucial.  While there is a significant amount of literature on recognizing objects from multiple views, scattering light interferometry makes it possible to create 3D visual information of objects without a camera, enabling the reconstruction of moving objects using light pattern interference.  We present a novel technique, called Diffraction Interference Based Object Recognition, that utilizes scattering light interferometry to create 3D visual information of objects and a deep learning framework to recognize objects from 3D information.  Our research demonstrates that our DIFFRACTION-IR network can effectively recognize objects even when partially hidden or in complex scenarios, outperforming traditional 2D image recognition by a significant margin, and can accurately identify objects that are fully hidden or heavily distorted.  Since this method uses 3D information, it is also resilient to rotation, scaling, and other forms of transformation.  Furthermore, it has the potential to be used in various applications, including surveillance systems, interactive games, and augmented reality technology.  One of the key advantages of our DIFFRACTION-IR network is that it can recognize objects without a background, making it an excellent option for recognizing objects in cluttered environments.  As the best known approach using scattering light interferometry at the time of publication, our Diffraction Interference Based Object Recognition research has the potential to significantly contribute to the field of vision-based object recognition.  We make our DIFFRACTION-IR dataset publicly available, consisting of 12,000+ images of objects reconstructed using scattering light interferometry, to facilitate further research.  As the first study using scattering light interferometry to recognize objects, our research paves the way for exploring various patterns of light interference, including diffraction, reflection, and diffusion, and encourages the development of new techniques for 3D visual information reconstruction.  We believe that our Diffraction Interference Based Object Recognition research will have a significant impact on the vision science community, enabling the creation of innovative technology, and paving the way for further research into 3D visual information reconstruction, recognition, and manipulation. While the frequency of specific word sequences has been extensively studied, the current research delves into the underlying underlying semantics, aiming to understand why these patterns exist in the first place.  Utilizing a large corpus of English text, we have discovered that the statistical properties of word sequences are closely tied to the semantic relationships between words, and a method to calculate this relationship has been developed.  By applying this technique to thousands of concepts, we have mapped out the network of semantic connections within the English language, and made the resulting graph available for public use.  This research has several implications, and potential uses include improving language generation, enhancing language processing capabilities, and providing a framework for creating multilingual dictionaries.  One notable discovery was that a significant portion of concept pairs exhibit reciprocal semantic relationships, indicating that the structure of language is largely bi-directional.  Furthermore, our findings suggest that many concepts have multiple interconnecting paths of varying strength, and that the most strongly connected concepts in English include 'woman' and'man', implying that the structure of language is free from significant biases.  However, we also found that concepts related to animals and food tend to be more strongly connected than those involving abstract ideas and emotions, which is consistent with evolutionary theories that language evolved to facilitate the transmission of useful information.  One possible explanation for the pattern of semantic relationships is that they reflect the diversity of human experiences and the ways in which concepts are perceived and categorized in the mind.  Additionally, our research has several limitations, and future studies could build on our findings by exploring the dynamics of semantic change over time, examining the cultural variability of concept relationships, and investigating the relationship between semantic and categorization theories. The algorithmic process begins with computing pre-images of the invariant set under system dynamics, which can be done efficiently using existing methods such as numerical resolution or linear programming depending on the system's characteristics. One concern with these methods is their reliability when scarce local data is available, which is a common scenario in many real-world applications.  To address this concern, we present a robust user-centered approach that incorporates partial local information when fine-tuning language models.  Our method, called LocalInformed, stands out from existing user-centered methods by utilizing partial local information to enhance the real-world data used for fine-tuning.  We demonstrate through extensive experiments on five real-world datasets (ATIS, SNIPS, Cambridge, ZeroShotRec, and 64A) that LocalInformed results in significantly improved performance when using small local datasets and significantly outperforms existing approaches.  We also investigate the efficacy of LocalInformed by varying the quality of real-world data used for fine-tuning and find that it consistently delivers high performance even with noisy real-world data.  One additional benefit of LocalInformed is its ability to provide well-informed representations when local information is substantial, which we verify through experiments.  We believe that LocalInformed has the potential to revolutionize real-world, low-resource speech applications and is available for use, having been implemented in an publicly accessible code repository.   Research in cognitive science has shown that people quickly recognize themes and concepts in music, yet the processes behind this recognition remain unclear.
  To address this knowledge gap, we propose an innovative framework that utilizes recurrent neural networks to recognize abstract concepts and musical themes.
  Our approach, which we call "Theme-Concept Embedding," enables the representation of themes and concepts as fixed points in a high-dimensional space, allowing for the calculation of distances between them.
  We have developed two variant models: the "Separate Model" and the "Shared Model," each capable of representing multiple themes and concepts, and have evaluated their performance using multiple datasets.
  The "Separate Model" achieved high accuracy in recognizing themes from a dataset used in a previous study, and could also recognize concepts from a dataset used in a different study.
  Additionally, this model demonstrated the ability to learn hierarchical representations of themes, and could recognize new instances of learned themes even when partially presented.
  The "Shared Model" successfully recognized both musical and non-musical themes/concepts, and could learn semantic relationships between concepts from textual descriptions.
  One dataset used in our research is available for public use, and we hope that our framework will contribute to the development of more effective music information retrieval systems.  Copyright 2020 Neural Information Processing Systems

Despite its potential for determining the carrier recombination mechanism, such experimentation has yielded conflicting results. To resolve this discrepancy, we conducted a comprehensive study using transient photoluminescence and transient absorption techniques. Upon analyzing the carrier decay curves obtained under various conditions, we observed a clear difference in recombination behavior between 3MECH perovskite and the more stable 3M perovskite structure. Transient photoluminescence measurements revealed bi-exponential decay in 3MECH, whereas transient absorption measurements showed a linear combination of two exponential functions in 3M. Furthermore, we discovered that trap-related recombination occurs within ~100 picoseconds in both materials, followed by defect-independent recombination that takes place on a much longer timescale in 3MECH compared to 3M. By simulating the recombination process and comparing the results with experimental data, we confirmed that the observed decay curves are consistent with a carrier recombination model involving both trap-related and defect-independent recombination mechanisms. In the 3MECH perovskite structure, this results in significantly delayed carrier decay on a millisecond timescale. As the most significant factor influencing carrier recombination, we found that unpaired electrons at metal cation sites are responsible for defect-independent recombination. Through density functional theory calculations, we established that unpaired electrons occur when unbalanced cation composition leads to cation vacancy formation. By eliminating unpaired electrons, we demonstrate that molecular decoration can significantly inhibit defect-independent recombination, thereby enhancing carrier lifetime in hybrid perovskites. Our first algorithm, which we call the "turning point algorithm," solves such systems by finding the turning points of specific curves defined within a Gr\"afserberian hypersurface.  We proved that this algorithm is correct, and that the set of turning points is finite.  Building on this result, we developed a second algorithm that calculates all solutions using the turning points found through the first algorithm.  Both algorithms have a polynomial time complexity in terms of the input's algebraic variety but an exponential time complexity in terms of the system's parameters.  We also presented an alternative variant of the turning point algorithm that calculates specific solutions quickly once the turning points have been discovered.  To demonstrate the efficiency of our algorithms, we compared our outcomes with existing methods for solving triangular systems.  In doing so, we observed that our algorithms outperformed these existing methods in various test cases.  One contribution of this research is the discovery that certain solutions to specific types of systems can be classified as "pseudo-almssen" or "true almsen" based on the location of the turning points' variety within a specific hypersurface.  Additionally, we proved that true almsen solutions are a necessary condition for systems with positive degree to have general solutions.  Furthermore, we established that true almsen solutions correspond to general solutions in systems with positive degree and satisfy specific algebraic equations.  Finally, we presented a way to calculate true almsen solutions using the turning point algorithm or alternatively through the elimination of variables. Despite the importance of this task, few studies have been devoted to generating reliable models of Earth's atmosphere for exoplanet research, particularly using laboratory data. This research is also part of a larger initiative called the ExoMOL project, whose goal is to provide high accuracy molecular line lists for exoplanet research and the study of cool star atmospheres.  This project involves a team of researchers from Italy, China, and the US working together to characterize the spectra of key atmospheric molecules through laboratory measurements and theoretical calculations.  The ExoMOL project aims to release the characterized data into the public domain to facilitate the creation of reliable models of exotic exoplanese atmospheres and the search for biosignatures.   To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel approach to optical meteor trajectory estimation, utilizing data from wide-field optical telescopes. This method, called Particle Filter Based Recursive Estimation, uses 2D sky images and prior knowledge of meteor characteristics to estimate trajectories. 

  Utilizing a particle filter algorithm to evaluate possible trajectories and Gaussian Mixture Models to represent the trajectory distribution, this method can handle non-linear motion and measurement uncertainties. After optimizing the proposal distribution and updating the trajectory estimate, it selects the most likely trajectory as the final estimate. 

  To evaluate this method, simulations were conducted using observed BBO and ATOMS meteor data and the proposed approach, showing promising results in both cases. Our focus was on the local degree-based approach, specifically for simple, undirected graphs without multiple edges. We introduced local graph properties, the local first and second graph spectrum, and defined the local characteristic polynomial. We also demonstrated that the local first and second graph spectrum are equivalent to the local characteristic polynomial's zeros and that the local first graph spectrum determines the local property. This research aims to contribute to this goal by providing an accurate estimate of the big bang neutrino temperature at early times.  We utilize a novel numerical method that efficiently evolves neutrino perturbations in the universe, and apply it to calculate the visible and invisible neutrino spectra through the process of neutrino oscillations, particularly within the context of the cosmological neutrino density puzzle.  Our results indicate that microripples in neutrino distributions, resulting from the interaction of neutrinos with large-scale matter perturbations, are a significant factor in filling the invisible neutrino spectrum.  Based on our research, we propose a revised estimate of the big bang neutrino temperature to be on the order of 0.70 to 0.73eV, with a possible margin of +/-0.05eV, in an effort to bridge the visible and invisible neutrino density curves.  We believe that the neutrino density puzzle is not inherently theoretical, but rather a manifestation of our current limitations in understanding the universe's initial conditions and the evolution of neutrino perturbations.  Our research advocates for the integration of full neutrino perturbation evolution into large-scale structure and cosmological simulations, and encourages the community to explore the phenomenon of neutrino oscillations in the presence of perturbations.  We hope that our research inspires a collaborative effort to rectify the visible and invisible neutrino density curves, and contributes to the development of a more accurate and mature understanding of the universe's initial conditions.  We make our numerical code, called Neutrino Initial Conditions Generator (NICGE), publicly available for the community's use and benefit.  The code is capable of evolving neutrino perturbations in various ways, including through the process of neutrino oscillations, and can be utilized to calculate visible and invisible neutrino spectra through the Boltzmann equation, as well as the 0.1eV to 10eV energy range of both visible and invisible neutrino species.  The code can also evolve neutrino perturbations in response to external perturbation scenarios, allowing users to study the evolution of neutrino perturbations in various environments, including foamy and clumpy conditions.  The code is compatible with various cosmological simulation codes, including the Einstein-Bartlett, Boltzmann-Einstein, and N-body simulation codes, and can generate initial conditions for both full and linear neutrino perturbation evolution scenarios

In experiments aiming to directly detect dark matter, this signal could be in the form of a low-energy photon, and the cavity's resonance frequency is crucial for identifying the particle's mass.  To determine the resonance frequency with high precision, the cavity's dimensions must be accurately known, which is challenging due to the microscopic scale of the cavity.  A possible approach to resolving this issue involves using a multiple-layer X-ray interferometry technique to measure the cavity's dimensions with a precision of $0.1$ nm.  However, the precision of this method is limited by the wavelength of the X-ray light used for interference, which constrains the measurement accuracy for extremely thin cavities.  To evaluate the practicality of this method, we have simulated various scenarios of measuring a $10$ $\mu$m thick cavity with an X-ray interference technique, which involves varying parameters such as the X-ray wavelength and the quality of the interference pattern.  By analyzing these simulations, we found that the most significant limitation of the technique is the minimum possible angle of X-ray reflection, which directly impacts the precision of dimension measurement.  We also explored alternative approaches to optimizing the measurement technique, including proposals to use a multi-layer X-ray interferometry with different arrangements of layers and the use of X-rays with a very small wavelength.  One simulation showed that using a layer arrangement that produces a resonant condition for X-ray interference can significantly improve the precision of dimension measurement by eliminating the boundary that restricts the minimum possible angle of X-ray reflection.  In the best-case scenario, the simulation indicated that it is possible to measure a $10$ $\mu$m thick cavity with a precision of $0.01$ nm, which is sufficient to meet the requirements of direct dark matter detection experiments for the simplest types of dark matter candidates but falls short of meeting the standards set by experiments targeting the best-candidate dark matter theory, which posits that the particle's mass is approximately $10^{-23}$ eV. Despite its prevalence, research on the theoretical properties of bootstrapping is scarce and often bypassed in published studies. This research fills that gap by providing a rigorous analysis of the theoretical characteristics of bootstrapping in ensemble learning.  Begining with an overview of the fundamental concepts, we delve into the theoretical examination of bootstrapping in both classification and regression contexts. In settings with repeated treatment decisions, previous research has established the importance of accounting for the influence of past treatments on the estimation of treatment effects.  However, when outcomes are also influenced by factors that predates the period in question, simply controlling for observed variables is insufficient.  We demonstrate that effects of current and past treatment variations are biased if the noise in treatment decisions is not properly modeled.  We further show that the local average treatment effect -- a common effect measure -- is specifically vulnerable to this issue.  To address this problem, we introduce a new effect measure: the recursive local average treatment effect.  We prove that this measure is unbiased when estimated using inverse propensity weightning, and demonstrate its utility using both theoretical examples and real-data simulations.  We also compare the recursive local average treatment effect to an alternative approach using instrumental variables, and find that it offers multiple advantages.  We believe that the recursive local average treatment effect has the potential to contribute to various research areas, including the analysis of policy effectiveness and the study of treatment effects on health outcomes.  This research extends the non-parametric treatment effect estimation framework, and is applicable in settings with both repeated and endogenous treatment decisions.  We provide an open-source software program on the journal's website that enables researchers to calculate the recursive local average treatment effect via inverse propensity weighting and bootstrap confidence intervals.  We also include a supplementary appendix that provides additional theoretical information, an overview of the estimation process, and a real-data case study on the effectiveness of job loss in improving health outcomes.  We make our code publicly available on the Econometrics Journal's data archive and on GitHub.  We observe that the recursive local average treatment effect via inverse propensity weighting has an integral connection with the instrumental variables approach, and note that it can be viewed as a local approximation of the instrumental variables effect.  We demonstrate that the most efficient estimator of the recursive local average treatment effect is the two-stage least squares estimator, and show that the difference between the instrumental variables effect and the recursive local average treatment effect is a measure of the noise in treatment decisions.  We provide a theoretical framework that enables researchers to calculate the variance of the recursive local average treatment effect via bootstrap resampling and Monte Carlo simulations.  We apply the recursive local average treatment effect to a real-data example on the effectiveness of smoking reduction in improving health outcomes, and demonstrate that it is possible to estimate the effect of extremely rare events (such as quitting smoking completely) using real-data.

As a result, it is possible to prevent the spread of viruses by modifying these tables proactively in response to emerging threats.  In a two-dimensional space where nodes are positioned along the x and y axes, a group of nodes that can communicate with each other are randomly dispersed.  Upon detection of a virus, there is a time delay before the infected node begins to spread the virus across the network.  The goal is to minimize the maximum amount of time a healthy node remains exposed to the virus in the network.  Using a model that includes infected and healthy nodes, an optimal real-time algorithm is available to recurve the routing tables and contain the virus's spread. Using a discrete probability distribution, the algorithm can make nearly perfectly informed decisions regarding how to recurve the routing tables.  A theoretical evaluation reveals that this algorithm can reduce the maximum time a healthy node remains exposed to the virus by at least an order of magnitude compared to the currentiest strategy of recuring the routing tables.  Through extensive simulations, the algorithm demonstrated a significant improvement over the currentiest strategy in various scenarios with different parameters.  This research contributes to our understanding of how to utilize SDN in containing the spread of viruses. As these searches cover a significant portion of the sky and are repeated multiple times, they are among the most widespread applications of neural networks in the world.  However, the stability requirements necessary to transmit and store these networks between sky observations are extremely high, preventing the use of the latest and most powerful models.  We propose a novel, compressed neural network architecture, called the Free Block Neural Network, which can be updated remotely and freely within a very narrow boundary of errors (less than 0.1\%) without the need for communication.  This new design exhibits a significant advantage over existing solutions, which typically have error margins of several percent.  After optimizing the initial training of the Free Block Neural Network and updating it incrementally, we achieved outstanding results on multiple data sets, including a public optical transient detection challenge where the model ranked at the very top.  The new design also demonstrates impressive performance compared to other popular compression techniques, which typically fall short in situations with limited lab data.  The free block structure allows for intuitive understanding and optimization, enabling the design to accommodate complex conditions and biases in the data without additional adjustments.  Furthermore, the Free Block Neural Network can be utilized in various scenarios, including the removal of known features, the handling of missing values, and the accommodation of different data sources and weights.  The code for the Free Block Neural Network is available on GitHub at https://github.com/sweenr/FBNN.  We anticipate the Free Block Neural Network to revolutionize the construction of neural networks for the search of faint optical transients and other rare events, and to pave the way for the use of even more powerful models in the future.  Additionally, the design can be applied in other domains where the storage and communication of neural networks are costly or difficult, such as edge computing, privacy concerns, and hardware limitations. alpha$,n)$^{26}$Mg reaction's cross-section is a crucial component in determining the stellar neutron capture cycle's pace.  Through a psychological experiment, researchers aimed to accurately measure this reaction's cross-section.  Five targets, each composed of a different isotopic form of magnesium, were exposed to a $^{23}$Na beam with varying intensities.  An organic detector recorded neutron spectra for each target, with data analyzed using the activation method to calculate corresponding cross-sections.  After processing over 10,000 activation curves, an average cross-section of 0.106$^{-20}$ eV was determined at a energy of 13.5 eV.  This measurement's precision (10%) is the most accurate to date, surpassing the necessary requirements for the stellar neutron capture cycle.  Additionally, the research team discovered an unexpected resonance in $^{26}$Mg at a energy of 13.5 eV, which could potentially impact the cycle's pace.  This finding suggests that further studies are necessary to fully comprehend the reaction's behavior.  The measured cross-section and resonance data can be utilized to develop more accurate models of the stellar neutron capture cycle.  In a closed system, the cycle's pace is approximately 50 times faster than the main s-process pathway, with a timescale of approximately 50,000 years.  However, in an asteroseismic context, the cycle's pace can vary significantly, with a timescale of anywhere between 10 and 100,000 years.  The measured cross-section and resonance data can also be used to evaluate the feasibility of using neutron capture logging as a seismic sensing method in future asteroseismology missions.  Such missions could potentially utilize a neutron source and detector within a few meters of a stellar surface, allowing for the creation of a resonance curve within a few hundred seconds.  With this technique, researchers estimate that they can measure stellar oscillations with amplitudes as small as 10$^{-7}$.  Furthermore, this method can provide high-precision data on stellar composition profiles, particularly for elements with rare isotopes.  Overall, this research contributes significantly to our understanding of the $^{23}$Na($\alpha$,n)$^{26}$Mg reaction and its implications for both the stellar neutron capture cycle and asteroseismology missions.   It is common for research to model voter behavior and election outcomes using game theory,
  particularly in situations involving multiple candidates and voters with preferences.
  However, when analyzing strategic voting, research often employs the simplistic model of voting
  where the winner is determined by a simple plurality of votes, ignoring issues with sincerity
  and truth-telling. This study addresses this limitation by exploring the topic through the
  lens of mechanism design, focusing on elections where voters cast sincere votes.
  The research investigates the feasibility of creating truthful voting mechanisms for single-win
  and multi-win elections, analyzing the possible outcomes in single-win and multi-win elections
  and examining the efficiency of outcomes in single-win elections. It is notable that in single-win
  elections, even though efficient outcomes can be achieved when voters have linear preferences,
  this is not possible when voters have preferences for majority cycles (e.g. among three candidates
  A, B, and C where A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A). In multi-win elections, outcomes can
  be efficient even with majority cycle preferences, demonstrating that the approach varies
  based on the winning conditions. The research also includes an analysis of the outcomes in three-way
  and larger multi-way elections, observing that outcomes can be efficient when voters have
  cyclical preferences but not necessarily in larger elections. Moreover, in three-way elections,
  outcomes can be efficient even with preferences for rotation (e.g. among three candidates A, B,
  and C where A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A).  It is also possible to achieve efficient
  outcomes through specific voting mechanisms in three-way elections with rotating preferences
  (e.g. alternative voting and Cox arbitration). In larger multi-way elections, outcomes can be
  efficient with rotating preferences when using specific voting mechanisms (e.g. Cox arbitration
  and Cox-Arrow arbitration).  The research contributes to the stream of studies on mechanism
  design for strategic voting, offering insights on the feasibility of truthful voting mechanisms
  for single-win and multi-win elections with various preference models.  The study provides a

  has been a longstanding issue. While local magnetic fields can be easily managed, their non-uniformity 
  poses a significant problem for sensing technology. In contrast, extremely large non-uniformities of 
  several milligradients are too small to affect the sensor's operation. Between these extremes, there 
  is a gap in our knowledge that this research aims to fill. We have employed a magnetic crust model, evacuating 
  free charges, and applying the Curie theorem to solve magnetic field problems in shapes defined by any 
  2D parameterization. A key discovery was that non-uniformities can propagate and scale with shape boundary 
  curvatures, potentially leading to extremely large gradients in narrow regions like the focus of a curved 
  magnetic sheet or a magnetic ring's interior. To mitigate these effects, it is essential to optimize shape 
  geometry. We propose a simple criterion: shaping the magnetic material to mirror the detector's geometry. 
  In the worst-case scenario, non-uniformities can exceed 10$^{-10}$ eV$\cdot$cm$^{-1}$, while optmizing 
  a rectangular sheet can reduce this value by a factor of 100. Furthermore, we found that non-uniformities 
  are highly anisotropic, varying significantly based on direction. To overcome this challenge, sensors 
  should be anisotropically oriented, reducing non-uniformities by a factor of 10$^4$ for certain shapes. 
  Ultimately, our research suggests that non-local magnetic fields are a minor concern for gravitational wave 
  detectors, and shaping the magnetic material optimally can effectively eliminate the effect. The most 
  extreme non-uniformity we observed was approximately 10$^{-8}$ eV$\cdot$cm$^{-1}$, while the highest 
  value that can be measured by advanced LIGO+ is on the order of 10$^{-13}$ eV$\cdot$cm$^{-1}$.  The

Noting that these massive structures extend over vast distances, we propose a new definition of a giant structure, focusing on the most extensive formations. Currently, this assessment is done visually, relying on the expertise of a cardiologist, which can be variable and vulnerable to errors.  Automating this process is crucial to meet clinical standards and the requirements of regulatory bodies.  Furthermore, with the increasing use of artificial intelligence in medical imaging, there is a established demand for robust, recurrent neural networks that can efficiently process high-resolution image data, yet these models often require substantial training data to function effectively, which poses a problem in the case of cardiac imaging as there is a limited amount of annotated data available.  To address these challenges, our study proposes a streaming, recurrent convolutional neural network architecture called DynamicFC, which utilizes both motion and still images to evaluate cardiac function, and we have demonstrated its effectiveness in a large, publicly available dataset, with results showing that it compares favourably to other state-of-the-art techniques.  In particular, we found that DynamicFC achieved high accuracy in distinguishing normal and impaired heart function, as well as in segmenting cardiac regions, and it did so with minimal oversight, implying a strong potential for clinical use, while also meeting the requirements of regulatory bodies.  Additionally, we observed that the model's residual connections played a crucial role in generating meaningful segmentations, and we demonstrated that by replacing these connections with linear layers, we could significantly improve the educability of the network, which is advantageous in the case of limited annotated data, which is a common scenario in real-world scenarios.  Finally, we have made our code publicly available to facilitate the reproduction of our results and further development of the architecture.  In conclusion, our DynamicFC architecture provides a strong foundation for the development of clinical applications for cardiac Cine MR imaging, which can be used to evaluate wall motion and assess cardiac function, and it has the potential to be extended to other medical imaging modalities and applications.  Furthermore, our results demonstrate that recurrent neural networks can be effectively used in emergency medical imaging scenarios, which is a breakthrough given the high computational costs associated with these models, and we have established that residual connections are essential in generating meaningful segmentations in cardiac imaging, which is a new contribution to the field. We also demonstrate that any closed curve in this space is a planar curve, and that any simple closed curve can be transformed into a circle through a uniform scaling and a rotation. Furthermore, we prove that the space's curvature can be maximized while keeping its volume constant, and that the space's curvature can be optimized in a way that its volume remains bounded and its curvature tends towards infinity as its diameter tends towards a specific value.  In a more general context, we establish that any regularly curved space that is uniformly similar to a part of a flat space in a higher-dimensional Euclidean space can be represented in a specific form, and that the curve's shape can be computed from its initial conditions. We also show that the space's curvature can be optimized while keeping its volume constant, and that the space's curvature can be optimized in a way that its volume remains bounded and its curvature tends towards infinity as its diameter tends towards a certain value.  This research has implications for various areas of study, including geometry, optimization problems, and bi-dimensional visualizations of regularly curved spaces. explosive materials concealed within luggage has always been a critical problem for transportation security systems.  Given the dangers of using potentially dangerous technology like X-ray backscatter for this purpose and the high cost of using multiple technologies like X-ray and neural detectors, there's a strong interest in using electromagnetic wave (EMW) technology to make these detections.  However, the effectiveness of deep learning-based anomaly detection methods like convolutional neural networks (CNN) on EMW images of luggage is heavily dependent on the quality of the training image data.  Since directly obtaining images of concealed anomalies is often impossible, an alternative approach is presented here, leveraging a physical model of EMW imaging to generate simulated training images.  Using a specific example of a concealed explosive material, a physical model of EMW imaging was used to create a large number of training images and evaluate the effectiveness of CNN in detecting it.  The results showed that, compared to other segmentation techniques like thresholding and active contour models, a CNN yielded significantly better detection results after optimization.  Additionally, an investigation into the factors affecting the quality of simulated training images revealed the importance of accounting for physical parameters like wavelength, shape, and size when using a physical model of EMW imaging.  Finally, the feasibility of using a physical model to create realistic training image scenarios was demonstrated, which is invaluable for evaluating the effectiveness of anomaly detection methods and optimizing existing ones.  The results of this research have significant implications for the development of effective anomaly detection methods for transportation security systems and other similar applications.  One contribution of this research is an open-source software tool called "WaveImaging" that utilizes a physical model of EMW imaging to generate simulated training images of concealed anomalies.  This tool can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of anomaly detection methods and optimize existing ones for various scenarios.  The results of this research also provide a foundation for the development of real-world systems for detecting concealed anomalies with EMW technology in various applications.  Another contribution of this research is a publicly available dataset called "WaveAnomaly" that utilizes a physical model of EMW imaging to simulate training images of concealed small animals.  This dataset is available online and can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of anomaly detection methods and optimize existing ones for various scenarios.  The results of this research demonstrate the effectiveness of using a physical model of EMW imaging to create realistic training image scenarios for developing effective anomaly detection methods.  The results also provide a foundation for the development of real-world systems for detecting concealed small animals with EMW technology in various applications.
