To better understand the evolution of small body asteroids through time, there is a need for a more in-depth understanding of how asteroids break apart in collisions.  Numerical simulations of asteroid impacts, which serve as the primary basis for understanding how asteroids evolve over time, are limited by their inaccuracy when modeling the initial conditions of small body asteroid collisions.  To address this issue, laboratory experiments have been conducted to investigate how icy planetesimals fracture in crushing collisions, which is presented in this research.  Using high-speed impactors made of a similar material to small body asteroids, experiments were performed on icy planetesimal analogs in a vacuum environment to observe how they fractured in oblique impacts.  The resulting fractures were carefully measured to create a dataset for numerical modeling purposes.  The results of the experiments reveal that icy planetesimals have a tendency to split along a plane that is perpendicular to the impactor's trajectory in oblique impacts, which is inconsistent with current collision models.  A new model, which takes into account the mechanical properties of icy planetesimals and how they fracture in crushing collisions, has been proposed to replace the existing impact simulation methodology.  This new model significantly reduces the energy lost in impacts and results in more massive asteroids breaking apart in collisions.  As a demonstration of the new model's effectiveness, numerical simulations of asteroid (1015) Arwacois and asteroid (52776) Muralintan were conducted to analyze how they evolved over time and compare the outcomes to existing models.  The results of the research suggest that a significant portion of small body asteroids with diameters between 1 and 10 kilometers in our solar system are likely composed of multiple fragments that originated from a single precursor asteroid.  As a byproduct of the research, a public dataset of fracture patterns in icy planetesimals has been made available for the scientific community to utilize.  According to the research, future studies on the evolution of small body asteroids through time and the formation of ring systems in planets should consider the proper simulation of fracture patterns in icy planetesimals in impact scenarios.  Additionally, the research proposes the following mission concepts to search for fragments of multiple asteroid systems in our solar system:  the Near-Earth Asteroid Scout (NEAS) mission, the Asteroid Impact and Exploration (AIDE) mission, and the Small Asteroid Rider (STAR) mission. We present an argument that the problem arises from using insufficient premises and provide an additional axiom, which we call the "Continuity Axion," to rectify the issue.  This new axiom is equivalent to a well-known theorem by Bolzano and involves a condition that can be graphically represented as a "nowhere-monotone" curve.  We also explore the implications of our new axiom and demonstrate that it is consistent, possibly even a theorem, within a specific model presented by KeHsenbrenner.  One contribution of this research is the observation that the Continuity Axion is more precise than an alternative solution proposed by Robinson.  Additionally, we analyze the relationship between the Continuity Axion and other axioms, including one presented by Ferrante, and examine its connection to a condition called "sigma-finiteness" in first-order logic.  We further investigate the scope of our new axiom, considering both general and specific cases, as well as its application in a formal system that utilizes infinitesimally small quantities, which we term "infinitesimal calculus." Another contribution is the development of a topology on the set of infinitesimally small numbers, which we call the "infinitesimal topology," and we prove that it is equivalent to the standard topology on an open interval presented in reverse order. Through the use of neutron diffusion imaging, we have discovered that the magnetic order in beta-FeO3 is anisotropic within individual grains.  Within the ab-plane, the magnetic order is uniform, however, along the c-axis, it exhibits a spin spiral pattern where adjacent layers' magnetic moments are aligned in an alternating pattern.  Theoretical calculations using the local spin density approximation agree with these findings and also revealed that the anisotropy is rooted in the imbalance of oxygen p-orbital bonding within the c-axis.  By manipulating this bonding through substitution, it is possible to influence the anisotropic magnetic properties, as seen in the examples of Mn and Cr substitution. To further understand these correlations, we investigated the shape of non-identical charged particle correlations in p+p and p+A collisions at moderate pseudorapidity densities, focusing on particles with opposite signs of charge.  These shapes were found to be similar in p+p and p+A collisions, but showed distinct differences between the two systems.  In both p+p and p+A collisions, non-identical charged particle correlations exhibited a characteristic "triangle" shape, with correlations peaking when particles were of moderate pseudorapidity separation.  However, in p+A collisions these correlations were found to be stronger and more pronounced than in p+p collisions, and could be described by a similar model used to explain non-identical particle correlations in heavy ion collisions.  These findings suggest that non-identical charged particle correlations in small system collisions originate from particle interaction mechanisms similar to those responsible for correlations seen in heavy ion collisions.  Additionally, we observed that these correlations are influenced by the presence of intermediate state resonances, and can serve as an indicator of particle multiplicity density variations with collision energy.  These results contribute to our understanding of non-identical charged particle correlations and their use in studying heavy ion collision behavior.  Furthermore, these correlations may also be useful in studying heavy ion collision behavior, and have the potential to aid in the development of heavy jet reconstruction methods.  In p+p and p+A collisions, non-identical charged particle correlations could be described by a combination of hadronic interaction models, but in heavy ion collisions these correlations hold value as a tool for jet identification and the study of heavy jet interactions.  By analyzing these correlations in heavy ion collisions through heavy jet decay products, we gathered evidence of heavy jet formation in these events.  The data collected in 2017 and 2018 at various heavy ion collision energies (200-5020 GeV) demonstrates that heavy jets can form in these events, and that their formation is influenced by heavy ion collision energy and the presence of heavy quarks. While the standard theory of turbulence-driven instability leading to subsonic wind inflation is widely accepted, there are uncertainties in the model's stability and variability.  To address these issues, we performed a linear stability analysis of the advection-diffusion equation modeling the wind accretion process.  By applying the analysis to a power-law gamma-ray spectrum and an electron energy distribution function, we identified a critical value for the parameter $\kappa_0$, which marks the boundary between stable and unstable conditions.  Our results demonstrate that the model's stability is influenced by the presence of a minimum point in the wind acretion rate curve and a critical value in the parameter $\theta_0$.  We found that, for a Schwarzschild black hole, the most unstable mode has a wavelength of approximately $10r_g$ and an e-folding time of around $10^8(r_g/v_s)^2$ seconds.  Furthermore, we observed that the stability of the model is linked to the formation of relativistic jets and the cooling behavior of the wind acretion process.  Our study provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the variability patterns observed in black hole binaries and the formation mechanisms of relativistic jets.  By contributing to our knowledge of the subsonic wind acretion rate around black holes, this research aims to facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of jet formation and black hole physics.  The research's findings are available for public use, along with the corresponding code, to facilitate the analysis of similar problems. Using a localized state picture and tight-binding models, we explain how zero energy states arise at the edge of the modified section and propagate throughout the rest of the ribbon.  Our theoretical findings are supported by density functional theory calculations.  A key parameter influencing the formation of zero energy states is the edge disorder, which can be caused by vacancies or the presence of metal atoms.  We observe that even slight disorders can significantly impact the formation of these states, and propose a possible scenario where they disappear entirely in heavily disordered situations.  Additionally, we investigate the effect of spin-orbit interaction on zero energy states, and find that it can lead to the opening of gaps in the zero energy level pair when strong enough.  A key advantage of using an edge-disordered graphene nanoribbon with a metal atom replacement model over other zero energy state models is the potential for bandgap engineering through control of edge conditions and the replacement atom species.  As this configuration is highly susceptible to chemical modification, we suggest that zero energy state-based devices could utilize a self-limiting growth technique to achieve optimal performance.  A possible application of this technique is in the fabrication of zero energy state transistors, which could exhibit high on-off ratio values by utilizing a zero energy state channel and a conventional semiconductor material.  Another possible application is in the creation of zero energy state-based sensors, which could demonstrate strong responses to edge disorders and/or replacement atom species through changes in zero energy state properties.  A scenario where zero energy state sensors could utilize an external electrical field to enhance zero energy state openings and/or gaps, leading to improved performance, is also explored.  Theoretical calculations demonstrate that zero energy state openings and/or gaps can be significantly enhanced through the application of an external electrical field, which can also help overcome the opening/gap opening threshold through frictional stress.  A possible mechanism where an external electrical field can enhance zero energy state openings/gaps is proposed, involving the polarization of edge-localized states and the weakening of edge disorders. As these applications continue to evolve, there is growing interest in arranging Josephson junctions in complex patterns.  While the patterned growth of Josephson junctions is a complex process, artificial intelligence (AI) technology has the potential to significantly enhance it by providing detailed 3D models of the material's optimal formation conditions.  To explore the feasibility of using AI to optimize this process, we conducted a thorough investigation of the factors influencing the patterned growth of YBa2Cu3O7-x (YBCO) Josephson junctions on lattice-shaped Laura-Lau fabricated NbN templates.  Our research reveals that the growth conditions can be optimized for intricate patterns by using a template with a NbN thickness of at least 30 nm and a Laura-Lau substrate temperature of 700 degrees C.  Furthermore, our findings suggest that AI-driven simulations are effective in determining the formation conditions for various patterned junction arrangements on NbN templates of varying thickness.  As a result, we successfully fabricated Josephson junctions in complex patterns on a template with a NbN thickness of 25 nm, demonstrating the effectiveness of using AI to optimize the growth process.  Our research paves the way for the creation of sophisticated patterns on thinner templates, enabling the development of more complex superconducting circuits and the exploration of novel physical phenomena.  Additionally, our findings are applicable to other superconducting materials, including Nb, Bi2Sr2CaCu2Ox, and FeSe, and can contribute to the design of advanced superconducting devices with various materials.  Finally, our research demonstrates that the patterned growth of Josephson junctions can be achieved on templates with a Laura-Lau substrate temperature of 700 degrees C, expanding the possible applications of this technique to the creation of superconducting devices that require high temperature stability, including the development of superconducting bolometers and the improvement of superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs). point process is a set of connections that links points, and it can be described as a graph. As a result, research has applied graph theory to analyze the structure of point processes, especially in the case of random processes. The statement that a point process is stationary in a given area and its topology is uniform across that area is known as the uniformity hypothesis. In a recent study, Boroczky and Kegeszmus investigated how the topology of a homogeneous Poisson process aligns within a rectangular area assuming the uniformity hypothesis holds [1]. Building on their findings, we explore how the topology of a homogeneous Poisson process relates within a polygonal area under the uniformity hypothesis. We derive a concise formula to determine if two given points are connected by an edge within such an area. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of specific scenarios, including a scenario where multiple Poisson processes overlap within a given area and a scenario where points are restricted to certain areas or barred from others. The uniformity hypothesis is also validated for a homogeneous Poisson process within a polygonal area through an established probability threshold. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the boundary of such a process's topology within a polygonal area can be represented as a collection of straight lines. Lastly, we observe that the uniformity hypothesis holds for a subset of locally finite, stationary point processes in a given area after the removal of a set of linearly related boundaries.  The research presented offers a comprehensive understanding of the topological connectivity of a homogeneous Poisson process within a polygonal area. It provides a foundation for further investigations into the topic. Moreover, the study extends the applicability of graph theory to the analysis of point processes. It also contributes to the development of strategic approaches in studying the connectivity of random point processes in a given area. The research is pertinent to various fields, including statistics, geometry, and computer science. It has practical applications in the analysis of wireless networks, animal scattering experiments, and geographic information systems. We present an approach to determine if a group G is free by examining local dimensions of subgroups of a generation set of G, and also provide a polynomial-time algorithm to compute local dimensions within groups of bounded width. Furthermore, we outline how local dimension theory can be employed to identify groups with infinite rank that are not contained in a free group of finite rank n for any positive integer n. We demonstrate the applicability of local dimension theory by analyzing the structure of graphical groups, particularly for graph families such as K_n, its partial line version, a semi-complete graph with 4 points, and a collection of graphs known as Delta-free graphs. Additionally, we derive conditions on the structure of a graph G to determine if the graphical group Gamma_G is free, along with an analysis of equivalent conditions including the absence of certain subgraphs, the local dimension of vertices within a representation of G, and the presence of certain subsets within a free basis of Gamma_G. Finally, we outline local dimension bounds for specific graph configurations and provide an example of a graph (in the form of a tree) whose graphical group has infinite local dimension.  This research contributes a novel characterization of groups with geometric complexity 2, and offers a comprehensive framework for describing free groups through the perspective of local dimension theory.  This work has implications for geometric group theory, particularly for the study of groups with geometric complexity 2, and provides a foundation for investigating similar topics within the field.  This research is dedicated to Romain Weispfenning.  Romain made significant contributions to geometric group theory, particularly in the study of graphical groups and the characterization of free groups through local dimension theory. Building on previous research, we examine the exponential growth of polymer size with decreasing temperature, and demonstrate that the volume occupied by the polymer in the most stretched conformation is directly proportional to the exponential growth.  A key finding shows that there is a specific temperature threshold below which polymers will inevitably overlap when aligned in their most stretched conformation, and that this threshold corresponds to an exponential growth of polymer size by a factor of 10 to the 10th power for every 1.4-fold increase in polymer size.  Additionally, we observe that the largest possible stretching factor along any dimension is directly proportional to the square root of the volume occupied by the polymer in its most stretched conformation and inversely proportional to the polymer's end-to-end distance.  A theoretical model is also provided to explain why the largest possible stretching factor is bounded by 10 to the 10th power for polymers of moderate size.  Finally, we demonstrate that the largest possible stretching factor along any dimension is at least proportional to the square root of the polymer size when aligned in its most stretched conformation and that the product of the largest possible stretching factors along any two dimensions is directly proportional to the polymer's surface area when aligned in its most stretched conformation.  A key contribution of this research is the establishment of a lower bound of 10 to the 50th power for the product of the largest possible stretching factors along any two dimensions for a polymer of 10 to the 20th power in size.
